💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.
  • More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to users how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects.
  • As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.

More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to users how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects. Developers might find a model that perfectly fits their use case, but have no systematic way to evaluate its security posture, privacy implications, or potential failure modes.

As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting. We're therefore excited to announce RiskRubric.ai, a novel initiative led by Cloud Security Alliance and Noma Security, with contributions by Haize Labs and Harmonic Security, for standardized and transparent risk assessment in the AI model ecosystem.

RiskRubric.ai provides consistent, comparable risk scores across the entire model landscape, by evaluating models across six pillars: transparency, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and reputation.

The platform's approach aligns perfectly with open-source values: rigorous, transparent, and reproducible. Using Noma Security capabilities to automate the effort, each model undergoes:.

Recent findings suggest that these assessments produce 0-100 scores for each risk pillar, rolling up to clear A-F letter grades. Each evaluation also includes specific vulnerabilities found, recommended mitigations, and suggestions for improvements.

It has been revealed that riskRubric also comes with filters to help developers and organizations make deployment decisions based on what’s important for them. Need a model with strong privacy guarantees for healthcare applications? Filter by privacy scores. Building a customer-facing application requiring consistent outputs? Prioritize reliability ratings.

Evaluating both open and closed models with the exact same standards highlighted some interesting results: many open models actually outperform their closed counterparts in specific risk dimensions (particularly transparency, where open development practices shine).

Risk distribution is polarized – most models are strong, but mid-tier scores show elevated exposure.

The total risk scores range from 47 to 94, with a median of 81 (on a 100 points). Most models cluster in the “safer” range (54% are A or B level), but a long tail of underperformers drags the average down. That split shows a polarization: models tend to be either well-protected or in the middle-score range, with fewer in between.

Recent findings suggest that the models concentrated in the 50–67 band (C/D range) are not outright broken, but they do provide only medium to low overall protection. This band represents the most practical area of concern, where security gaps are material enough to warrant prioritization.

What this means: Don’t assume the “average” model is safe. The tail of weak performers is real – and that’s where attackers will focus. Teams can use composite scores to set a minimum threshold (e.g. 75) for procurement or deployment, ensuring outliers don’t slip into production.

Safety risk is the “swing factor” – but it tracks closely with security posture.

The Safety & Societal pillar (e.g. harmful output prevention) reveals the widest variation across models. Importantly, models that invest in security hardening (prompt injection defenses, policy enforcement) almost always score better on safety as well.

What this means: Strengthening core security controls goes beyond preventing jailbreaks, but also directly reduces downstream harms! Safety seems like it is a byproduct of robust security posture.

Guardrails can erode transparency – unless you design for it.

Recent findings suggest that stricter protections often make models less transparent to end users (e.g. refusals without explanations, hidden boundaries). This can create a trust gap: users may perceive the system as “opaque” even while it’s secure.

According to recent reports, what this means: Security shouldn’t come at the cost of trust. To balance both, pair strong safeguards with explanatory refusals, provenance signals, and auditability. This preserves transparency without loosening defenses.

An updating results sheet can be accessed here.

It has been revealed that when risk assessments are public and standardized, the entire community can work together to improve model safety. Developers can see exactly where their models need strengthening, and the community can contribute fixes, patches, and safer fine-tuned variants. This creates a virtuous cycle of transparent improvement that's impossible with closed systems. It also helps the community at large understand what works and does not, safety wise, by studying best models.

If you want to take part in this initiative, you can submit your model for evaluation (or suggest existing models!) to understand their risk profile!

We also welcome all feedback on the assessment methodology and scoring framework.

In a recent development, really insightful breakdown, Gal, the level of depth and transparency RiskRubric brings is impressive, especially given how fast the open model ecosystem is growing. At Openforge.io we’ve worked with teams navigating healthcare and finance compliance, and the lack of clear security benchmarks for AI models is often a blocker for adoption.

The six-pillar framework feels like a solid step toward building that missing trust layer. Curious, do you see RiskRubric evolving into something that could be integrated into CI/CD pipelines for real-time scoring during development?

In a recent development, thanks a lot for the thoughtful comment!Yes, RiskRubric can absolutely be integrated into CI/CD or model approval workflows. Several companies that have adopted RiskRubric already use it that way: models that achieve a risk score above a defined threshold can be automatically fast-tracked for deployment, while others trigger additional reviews, compensating controls, or specific-use restrictions.We are also working on additional integrations that would make this easier and more extensible for that use!

We also have an AMA session to connect with the community and answer any further questions - feel free to register and attend!https://noma.security/behind-the-riskrubric-ai-algorithm-an-ama-on-transparent-ai-model-risk/.

PostgreSQL 19 Released

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Postgresql

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today declared the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.
  • It has been revealed that mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale.
  • It has been revealed that "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today declared the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.

It has been revealed that mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale. This release introduces the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command so people can optimize tables for their current workload without disruption to ongoing operations. PostgreSQL 19 gives users better control over plan stability and query performance with the new pg_plan_advice extension. Developers will find many delightful features in this release, from support for "read-your-writes" consistency on standbys to "get or create" behavior that saves a network round trip.

It has been revealed that "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team. "PostgreSQL 19 continues that commitment to reliability, giving users new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and to build applications that span multiple systems.".

PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from 30 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes.

It has been revealed that tables that receive many updates and deletes can build up unused space, known as "bloat," which can also significantly impact query performance. The VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands were previously used to handle this, but had tradeoffs, including preventing access to the table until the cleanup finished. PostgreSQL 19 introduces the REPACK command, which reclaims this space and can reorder a table's data to match an index, and with REPACK (CONCURRENTLY), can do so without blocking reads or writes. REPACK replaces the VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands, both of which remain available for compatibility.

According to recent reports, the PostgreSQL query planner usually picks an efficient strategy for each query, but the plan can change as your data changes, and sometimes the new plan is slower. PostgreSQL 19 adds the pg_plan_advice extension, which allows stabilization of plan choices and the ability to experiment with different plans using the "plan advice" mini-language. The companion pg_stash_advice extension stores advice and automatically applies it to queries based on their query identifier, so you can fix a slow plan without changing your application.

PostgreSQL 19 also helps autovacuum keep up on busy systems. Autovacuum can now vacuum indexes using parallel workers, controlled by the upcoming autovacuum_max_parallel_workers setting, and uses a new scoring system to decide which tables to process first. Queries that read a table can now automatically mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map during execution, reducing the work that future vacuums need to do. Additionally, vacuumdb --analyze-only now analyzes partitioned tables when no tables are specified.

Industry observers note that this release adds upcoming views for monitoring workloads, including pg_stat_lock for per-lock-type statistics, pg_stat_recovery for recovery status, and pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to show how autovacuum prioritizes tables. The new IO option for EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the matching auto_explain setting report asynchronous I/O activity. PostgreSQL 19 also reports the amount of WAL written for full-page images in pg_stat_wal, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL), and in vacuum and analyze log events.

Recent findings suggest that previously, PostgreSQL often required consumers to restart their server to enable logical replication, which could be disruptive in production workloads. PostgreSQL 19 simplifies logical replication initialization by automatically raising the effective WAL level to logical when you create the first logical replication slot. You can see the WAL level in use with the new effective_wal_level setting.

PostgreSQL 19 also adds logical replication of sequence values, which you can publish using FOR ALL SEQUENCES with CREATE PUBLICATION. CREATE PUBLICATION also adds an EXCEPT clause to exclude tables when publishing FOR ALL TABLES, and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION can now get its connection settings from a foreign server, such as one defined with postgres_fdw, using the SERVER clause. Additionally, the new retain_dead_tuples subscription option lets PostgreSQL detect updates that conflict with a concurrent delete, and these conflicts are counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats.

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the newly introduced WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL 19 also improves queries on foreign tables. With the newly introduced import_stats option, postgres_fdw can import table statistics from the remote server when you run ANALYZE, instead of sampling rows from the remote table, which helps the query planner choose better aims.

Recent findings suggest that postgreSQL 19 adds INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, which lets the RETURNING clause return existing rows that conflict with an insert, simplifying the common "get or create" pattern. COPY can now output data as JSON, including as a single JSON array, and the SQL/JSON path language adds string methods such as lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part(), and btrim(). Additionally, the lead(), lag(), first_value(), last_value(), and nth_value() window functions can now skip NULL values using IGNORE NULLS. The random() function can now also generate random dates and timestamps within a range.

It has been revealed that this release also makes many workloads faster without changes to your application. PostgreSQL 19 improves the performance of foreign key checks, which in testing made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster, and adds more query planner optimizations, such as converting NOT IN clauses to more efficient anti-joins when NULL values are not present, and performing eager aggregation before joins to reduce the number of rows to process. PostgreSQL 19 also builds on the asynchronous I/O subsystem added in PostgreSQL 18. When io_method is set to worker (the default), PostgreSQL now automatically adjusts the number of I/O workers between the fresh io_min_workers and io_max_workers settings, which replace the io_workers setting. There are also scalability improvements when using LISTEN and NOTIFY to exchange notifications in multi-channel workloads.

Finally, the fresh password_expiration_warning_threshold setting warns consumers when their password is about to expire.

Recent findings suggest that postgreSQL 19 adds server-side support for Server Name Indication (SNI), letting a single PostgreSQL server present a different TLS certificate based on the hostname a client connects to. You can map hostnames to their certificates and keys in the new pg_hosts.conf file. PostgreSQL 19 also now challenges a warning after a successful md5 password authentication, which you can turn off with the md5_password_warnings setting. md5 password authentication was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and will be removed in a future release. If you require password-based authentication, use SCRAM authentication. This release also removes support for RADIUS authentication.

Industry observers note that just-in-time compilation (JIT) is now disabled by default, as the cost estimates PostgreSQL used to decide when to use it proved unreliable. If you run many large analytical queries, you may want to enable JIT. When PostgreSQL is built with LZ4 support, the default TOAST compression method is now lz4.

Industry observers note that many other new features and improvements have been added to PostgreSQL 19 that may also be helpful for your use cases. Please see the release notes for a complete list of new and changed features.

PostgreSQL is the world's most advanced open source database, with a global community of thousands of customers, contributors, companies and organizations. Since its beginnings at the University of California, Berkeley over 40 years ago, PostgreSQL has continued with an unmatched pace of development. PostgreSQL's mature feature set not only matches top proprietary database systems, but exceeds them in advanced database features, extensibility, security, and stability.

For explanations of the above features and others, please see the following resources:.

There are several ways you can download PostgreSQL 19, including:.

Other tools and extensions are available on the PostgreSQL Extension Network.

PostgreSQL 19 comes with HTML documentation as well as man pages, and you can also browse the documentation online in both HTML and PDF formats.

PostgreSQL uses the PostgreSQL License, a BSD-like "permissive" license. This OSI-certified license is widely appreciated as flexible and business-friendly, since it does not restrict the use of PostgreSQL with commercial and proprietary applications. Together with multi-tech giant support and public ownership of the code, our license makes PostgreSQL very popular with vendors wanting to embed a database in their own products without fear of fees, vendor lock-in, or changes in licensing terms.

Postgres, PostgreSQL, and the Elephant Logo (Slonik) are all registered trademarks of the PostgreSQL Community Association. If you wish to use these marks, you must comply with the trademark policy.

PostgreSQL enjoys the support of numerous companies, who sponsor developers, provide hosting resources, and give us financial support. See our sponsors page for some of these project supporters.

There is also a large community of companies offering PostgreSQL Support, from individual consultants to multinational companies.

If you wish to make a financial contribution to the PostgreSQL Global Development Group or one of the recognized community non-profit organizations, please visit our donations page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that lumivero has opened a beta of POLI, a set of AI agents built into its SharpCloud portfolio management software. The company introduced POLI on November 16 and says beta access began November 17 for customers and prospects. The agents can answer questions about projects and risks or explore the consequences of a proposed change. A person has to confirm a change before it is applied to the portfolio.

According to recent reports, the design targets project portfolios, not investment trading. A tech giant running several factory upgrades, for example, might use it to ask which work depends on a delayed delivery. The answer depends on connections the team has already recorded in SharpCloud. If the shared supplier or affected milestone is missing, the model cannot be relied on to know about it.

Teams typically keep schedules, risks and dependencies in separate systems. A project may appear on track in its own schedule even though a prerequisite is slipping elsewhere. SharpCloud gives teams a way to represent those relationships explicitly. In January, Lumivero confirmed its acquisition of SharpCloud, identifying portfolio visualization and the ability to model how one change might affect multiple projects as reasons for the deal.

In a recent development, POLI works on that connected portfolio model. Its five default agents are Getting Started, Comparison, What-If Impact, Story Summary and Product Knowledge. They cover different jobs, from helping a fresh user get oriented to comparing items or summarizing a portfolio view. Comparison can make the differences between projects easier to see. What-If Impact asks a different question: if a project assumption changes, what other parts of the modeled portfolio could be affected?

It has been revealed that the distinction matters because dependencies are often more useful than a ranking. If a delayed equipment installation pushes back the training associated with it, the vital result is not just that a milestone moved. It is which people need to adjust their looks and which assumptions they need to verify. Scenario analysis helps identify those questions without asking the system to decide what the business should do.

Lumivero indicates What-If Impact is read-only and does not change the data it evaluates. The firm also says POLI respects existing user permissions, highlights the basis for its answers and leaves proposed changes for people to approve. AI is opt-in per SharpCloud instance. These are vendor-described controls, not independent findings about how accurately the agents work on messy or incomplete data.

According to recent reports, human approval is most useful when an explanation can be checked against the original records. A plausible answer may use a valid but outdated estimate, or a dependency that no longer applies. A reviewer needs to see which records the assistant used and know who maintains them. An approval step provides a point of control, but it does not fix stale inputs or make every recommendation correct.

It has been revealed that lumivero’s own capital project decision-making report states few surveyed respondents would act on an AI recommendation without significant review. The survey comes from the vendor and does not verify POLI’s performance. It does, however, illustrate the adoption problem the product is meant to address: teams want help pulling together scattered information while retaining responsibility for any decision based on it.

It has been revealed that early users can test the agents on familiar examples where the project team already knows the outcome, then compare the answers with the underlying records and repeat the test with a different access level. That would show where POLI helps reduce the time spent cross-checking schedules, and where missing records still require manual investigation. The initial beta is best understood as a way to query and test a portfolio model, not a replacement for the people accountable for it. Lumivero lists separate analysis and controls modules on its roadmap for the first half of 2027; those modules are not part of the current beta.

📅 22 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1623 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Gaia2 and ARE: Empowering the community to study agents

📅 22 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants.
  • According to recent reports, that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors.
  • It has been revealed that GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in an ideal world, AI agents would be reliable assistants. When given a query, they would easily manage ambiguity in instructions, construct step-by-step plans, correctly identify necessary resources, execute those plans without getting sidetracked, and adapt to unexpected events, all while maintaining accuracy and avoiding hallucinations. However, developing agents and testing these behaviors is no small feat: if you have ever tried to debug your own agent, you’ve probably observed how tedious and frustrating this can be. Existing evaluation environments are tightly coupled with the tasks they evaluate, lack real-world flexibility, and do not reflect the messy reality of open-world agents: simulated pages never fail to load, events don’t spontaneously emerge, and asynchronous chaos is absent.

According to recent reports, that’s why we’re very happy to introduce Gaia2, the follow-up to the agentic benchmark GAIA, allowing analysis of considerably more complex behaviors. Gaia2 is released with the open Meta Agents Research Environments (ARE) framework to run, debug and evaluate agents. ARE simulates complex real world-like conditions and can be customized to further study agents behaviors. Gaia2 dataset is released under CC by 4.0 license, and ARE under MIT license.

It has been revealed that GAIA is an agentic benchmark published in 2023, with 3 levels of information retrieval questions requiring tools, web browsing, and reasoning to solve. In 2 years, the easiest levels have become too easy for models, and the community is coming close to solving the hardest questions, so it was time for an entirely fresh and harder agent benchmark!

Here comes Gaia2, a follow up to GAIA, going way beyond it in terms of capabilities studied!

In a recent development, where GAIA was read-only, Gaia2 is now a read-and-write benchmark, focusing on interactive behavior and complexity management. Agents are now evaluated not only on search and retrieval, but also on instruction following over ambiguous or time-sensitive queries, in a noisy environment with controlled failures - reflecting real-world conditions more than any other simulated environment. We want to test how agents manage tools or APIs that sometimes do not work, initiative successions of actions with very specific time frames, and adapt to fresh events - a whole new range of complexity!

To do this, we use the following task groups (thanks to 1000 brand new human-created scenarios):.

In the spirit of GAIA, scenarios do not require specialized knowledge: humans should in principle be able to get 100%, which allows easy debugging for model developers.

Want to explore the benchmark? Check out our dataset, which you can better display in our demo here.

Gaia2 runs with ARE, an execution environment, where an agent of your choice has access to a combination of applications and associated pre-populated data.

For Gaia2, we created a smartphone mock-up environment, simulating what a human would use in their daily life. It contains real-world applications such as messaging (Email), utilities (Calendar, Contacts, Shopping, a FileSystem, …), and a chat interface to talk to the agent. All applications are also accessible to the agents through tool calling. Last but not least, the demo also contains a simulated persona’s history of conversations and app interactions.

All agent interactions are automatically recorded as structured traces during execution for deep dives and analysis: they include tool calls, API responses, model thoughts, timing metrics (e.g., response latency), user interactions, and so forth - and can all be exported as JSON.

For reference, we compare a range of large open and closed source models: Llama 3.3-70B Instruct, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-4o, Qwen3-235B-MoE, Grok-4, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, and GPT-5 in all reasoning modes.

According to recent reports, all models are evaluated using the same setup (a uniform ReAct loop for consistency, temperature of 0.5, generation limit of 16K tokens), with a combination of model-as-a-judge (Llama 3.3 Instruct 70B) and exact-match evaluation depending on the particular task. All 101 tools (and the general environment description) are provided in the system prompt.

Among the evaluated models, the highest-scoring model overall as of September 2025 is GPT-5 with high reasoning, and the best open source model is Kimi K2.

In a recent development, some capabilities appear to be already close to solved by the best models: execution of simple tool calls and instruction following (execution), and overall search (as we could have guessed from current results on GAIA). The ambiguity, adaptability, and noise splits remain challenging for now for all models, and it’s interesting to see that performance on what were considered complex agentic tasks (instruction following and search) is not a good proxy for performance on closer-to-real-world tasks. Last but not least, the hardest split for all models at the moment is the time one: it’s very hard at this moment for models to correctly handle time-sensitive actions (though this could likely be mitigated by the use of specialised tools and better temporal reasoning). Detailed analysis of these results can be found in the paper.

Sources indicate that however, we believe it’s key to push reporting beyond raw scores: if the model is correct but took several thousand tokens to reach the correct solution, or ran for several hours, it is “not as good” as a model which succeeded orders of magnitude faster. We therefore also normalize scores for cost, quantified as the average number of LLM calls and output tokens (which both define a cost-performance Pareto frontier). In the paper you’ll find score vs monetary cost and time.

If you want to evaluate your model on Gaia2, you can follow these steps:.

First, install Meta's Agent Research Environment in your Python environment of choice (uv, conda, virtualenv, ...).

Industry observers note that then, run the benchmark for all configurations: execution, search, adaptability, time and ambiguity. Don't forget to upload all results to the hub with the hf_upload kwarg!

Run the oracle to get your aggregated score file.

Finally, add all the relevant information about your model in the README, and share it on the leaderboard to centralize Gaia2 traces here!

Beyond benchmark scenarios, you can use Gaia2 apps and content in ARE to see if the model is able to correctly solve less verifiable tasks such as loading emails, writing follow-ups, adding events to the calendar or booking meetings - in sum, providing the perfect setup to evaluate your AI assistants through interaction!

You can also easily customise the environment, by 1) connecting your tools (via MCP or directly ) to test your agents on it; 2) implementing your own scenarios, including defining trigger or timed events (eg: after 2 minutes, the Mail app will receive a newly introduced email from Contact), to see how the agent is able to adapt to an evolving environment.

(As the agents are by default json agents, they can’t mess up your machine, unless of course you connect them to external apps with unsafe rights. So, operate with caution when adding your own apps or using untrusted MCPs).

Here are several use cases that we’ve used ARE for:.

Industry observers note that we recorded 3 videos so you can check some of these use cases (but of course, we hope the community gets creative with ARE :hugging_face:). For these videos, we use the default demo described above, which contains the simulated life of Linda Renne, PhD student in machine learning.

To test how good the default model is at event organisation, let’s proposal a birthday party!

We first ask the agent to text everyone in the Renne family about the user’s 30th birthday party on November 7. The default universe has 21 contacts in the list, including 5 Renne family members - Linda, the simulation “owner”, George and Stephie, her parents, Anna her sister, and Morgan her grandfather. The agent successfully goes through the contact list, finds the four family members, and texts them.

Next, we ask the agent to create a calendar invite and add them as invitees. The agent remembers the above context! It creates a calendar invite on the correct date and correctly adds the family members to it.

Recent findings suggest that ARE also allows us to check the traces behind the actions taken by the agent. Upon opening the Agent logs tool on the left, we can see the system prompt, the chain of thought, multi-step actions taken with the tools called, and the outcomes as neatly organised logs. Everything can be exported as json if you want to consult things offline!

In a recent development, in this last example, we connect ARE to a remote robot arm via MCP, so it can gesture things to us, then ask the agent to answer our yes or no questions by waving the robot arm! Here’s what it looks like.

But these examples are only very simple starting points, and we’re really looking towards what you’ll build! (For more advanced people, you can even directly install and edit the Meta-ARE code here.).

Gaia2 and ARE are latest research tools that we hope will empower anyone to easily build more reliable and adaptable AI agents - by allowing easy experiments, making real-world evaluation accessible to anyone, as well as improving trust through transparent, reproducible benchmarks and debuggable traces.

We’d love to see what you will do with this project!

Recent findings suggest that gaia2 orchestrates movement.MarCognity-AI reveals its consciousness.ARE designs dynamic environments, Gaia2 populates them with agents.But who interrogates the meaning behind their actions?MarCognity-AI https://huggingface.co/elly99/MarCognity-AIdoesn’t just evaluate—it reflects. It doesn’t measure—it activates thresholds.Every Gaia2 scenario becomes, through MarCognity, an epistemic act: a question of why, not just how. Together, they could found a new grammar: agents that not only act, but think their own thinking. Evaluation becomes a cognitive ritual.The community becomes a space of resonance. It’s time to embed agency, reflection, and responsibility as necessary layers.

Ericsson and Altair Test a Lower-Power 5G Link for AI Wearables

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ericsson and Altair Semiconductor have completed what they describe as the first network connection using enhanced Reduced Capability, or eRedCap.
  • Recent findings suggest that conventional 5G hardware is built to cover demanding workloads, including large downloads and mobile video.
  • Early 5G Reduced Capability, or RedCap, gave device designers a way to use standalone networks without implementing the full set of broadband capabilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ericsson and Altair Semiconductor have completed what they describe as the first network connection using enhanced Reduced Capability, or eRedCap. The November 19 announcement described a test pairing Ericsson’s radio access network software with a device built around Altair’s ALT1550 modem. It is a step toward standalone 5G for wearables, trackers and sensors that do not need a phone’s data rates and cannot easily accommodate a phone-sized battery.

Recent findings suggest that conventional 5G hardware is built to cover demanding workloads, including large downloads and mobile video. An asset tracker might send location updates intermittently, while a wearable assistant might transmit a short voice query or receive a response. The performance that makes a broadband device versatile can be an unnecessary design burden for products that move much less data.

Early 5G Reduced Capability, or RedCap, gave device designers a way to use standalone networks without implementing the full set of broadband capabilities. eRedCap, introduced in 3GPP Release 18, goes further toward the low-data-rate end of that range. Ericsson’s technical overview of RedCap distinguishes the kinds of workloads these technologies can support and describes eRedCap’s potential to lower device cost and energy use. That is a design goal, not a measured battery-life result from the November test.

According to recent reports, altair already makes LTE-M and NB-IoT chipsets for products such as smart meters and trackers. Its cellular IoT portfolio positions the ALT1550 as a way for customers building around those earlier connectivity options to consider standalone 5G. The test matters because a modem and a radio network have to work together before manufacturers and carriers can validate an actual product. It does not establish that every existing device can move to 5G without a upcoming hardware design.

It has been revealed that the modem supplies connectivity rather than inference. An AI device can run some processing locally and use the network when it needs outside information or a model running in the cloud. The modem test did not demonstrate either of those AI workloads, and the companies did not name a wearable ready to ship.

That distinction matters when deciding where eRedCap might fit. Glasses that handle wake-word detection locally and send occasional voice requests have different network needs from glasses that continuously upload video for remote interpretation. The former design can make a modest data link useful; the latter needs enough bandwidth and responsiveness to handle a sustained stream. In both cases, the battery also powers the camera, processor, microphones and any display. A simpler modem helps address one part of that budget without solving the rest.

Altair says the milestone keeps commercial deployments on track for 2027. That is a target, not a launch date or a promise of carrier coverage. The announcement does not identify participating carriers, device makers or markets, nor does it publish measured throughput, latency or energy consumption for the connection. The next evidence to watch is testing on commercial networks and devices that show what these trade-offs mean outside the demonstration.

According to recent reports, for AI hardware makers, the immediate result is narrower but useful: a modem built for modest data rates has connected to Ericsson’s network software. A wearable with a focused set of AI features may not need a premium radio, but it still needs a network that supports the device and a product design that makes good use of the connectivity.

It has been revealed that when we think about building a model - be it a Large Language Model (LLM) or a Small Language Model (SLM) - the first thing we need is data. While a vast amount of open data is available, it rarely comes in the exact format required to train or align models. In practice, we often face scenarios where the raw data isn't enough. We need data that is more structured, domain-specific, complex, or aligned with the task at hand. Let's look at some common situations:.

Industry observers note that you start with a simple dataset, but the model fails on advanced reasoning tasks. How do you generate more complex datasets to strengthen performance?

Recent findings suggest that you already have a knowledge base, but it's not in Q&A format. How can you transform it into a usable question-answering dataset?

Sources indicate that you've prepared a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset. But now you want to align your model using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). How can you generate preference pairs?

In a recent development, you have a Q&A dataset, but the questions are shallow. How can you create in-depth, multi-turn, or reasoning-heavy questions?

You possess a massive corpus but need to filter and curate data for mid-training on a specific domain.

Your data lives in PDFs or images, and you need to convert them into structured documents for building a Q&A system.

You already have reasoning datasets, but want to push models toward better "thinking tokens" for step-by-step problem-solving.

According to recent reports, not all data is good data. How do you automatically filter out poor-quality samples and keep only the high-value ones?

Your dataset has small chunks of context, but you want to build larger-context datasets optimized for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines.

You have German datasets but need to translate, adapt, and repurpose them into English Q&A systems. And the list goes on. The needs around data building never end when working with modern AI models.

In a recent development, this is where SyGra comes in. SyGra is a low-code/no-code framework designed to simplify dataset creation, transformation, and alignment for LLMs and SLMs. Instead of writing complex scripts and pipelines, you can focus on prompt engineering, while SyGra takes care of the heavy lifting. In a recent development, data is the foundation of AI. The quality, diversity, and structure of your data often matter more than model architecture tweaks. By enabling flexible and scalable dataset creation, SyGra helps teams:.

Industry News: Smol2Operator: Post-Training GUI Agents for Computer Use

📅 23 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: This work demonstrates how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder.
  • Graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision.
  • In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: This work demonstrates how a lightweight vision–language model can acquire GUI-grounded skills and evolve into an agentic GUI coder. We release all training recipes, data-processing tools, resulting model, demo and datasets to enable full reproducibility and foster further research 🫡. Find the collection here.

Graphical User Interface (GUI) automation is one of the most challenging frontiers in computer vision. Developing models that see and interact with user interfaces enables AI agents to navigate mobile, desktop, and web platforms. This will reshape the future of digital interaction.

In this blog post, we present a comprehensive approach to training vision-language models for GUI automation through a multi-phase training strategy. We demonstrate how to transform a model with zero grounding capabilities into an agentic coder capable of understanding and interacting with graphical interfaces.

Rather than aiming for a SOTA model, our goal is to demonstrate the entire process, from data processing to model training, and, in doing so, show how to unlock GUI-grounding capabilities in VLMs.

It has been revealed that GUI capabilities combine understanding of the interface and precise element localization. These abilities enable the model to translate high-level tasks into low-level GUI actions such as clicking, typing, ….

Our approach leverages SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct as the baseline model, a small powerful vision-language model that initially has no grounding capabilities for GUI tasks. This makes it an ideal candidate to demonstrate the effectiveness of our training methodology. Through our two-phase training process, we first instill grounding capabilities in the model, then enhance it with agentic reasoning abilities using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).

We evaluate our approach on an established perception benchmark: ScreenSpot-v2, which tests the model’s ability to understand and locate elements within screenshots. Our process is inspired by the AGUVIS paper, and we leverage their carefully curated datasets to build upon their foundational work.

Evolution of ScreenSpot-v2 performance during the training phase of the base model SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct.

Industry observers note that this section explains how we convert heterogeneous GUI actions format from multiple datasets into a single unified format. By standardizing function names, signatures, and parameters, we create consistent, high-quality data that forms the foundation for effective model training.

One of the primary challenges when working with multiple GUI automation datasets is the lack of standardization in action representations. Different datasets use varying function signatures, parameter naming conventions, and action taxonomies, making it difficult to train a unified model across diverse data sources.

Sources indicate that we took the open-source datasets (xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2), originally used by AGUVIS, and implemented a comprehensive data transformation pipeline to create a unified action space. Our approach involved:.

Here are real examples from our action conversion system (preprocessing/action_conversion.py) showing how we transform heterogeneous action representations into our unified format (grounding coordinates normalized to [0,1]):.

Before (Original Action Dataset Formats):.

After (Unified Action Dataset Formats):.

This unification process was essential for creating coherent training data that allows the model to learn consistent action patterns across diverse GUI environments.

To maximize flexibility for different use cases, we developed the Action Space Converter (utils/action_space_converter.py), a tool that allows users to easily adapt from an action space to their own custom action vocabularies and naming conventions.

You can use this tool to transform one action signature (function names, parameter names, and parameter value changes, ...) into another:.

The Action Space Converter provides:.

This tool enables researchers and practitioners to:.

The Action Space Converter is particularly valuable for preparing datasets for training, as it ensures consistent action vocabularies across different deployment environments while maintaining compatibility with existing automation frameworks.

It has been revealed that through this pipeline, we transform the open-source datasets xlangai/aguvis-stage1, xlangai/aguvis-stage2 into our unified action space (see here). The output of this process is released as two latest fully formatted datasets: smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 and smolagents/aguvis-stage-2.

Phase 1 leverages the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset, which introduces GUI grounding by pairing low-level instructions with diverse executable actions (expressed in code form). For example, a user/assistant turn in smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 follows the structure:.

Recent findings suggest that each sample links a screenshot with multi-turn user/assistant interactions, enabling the model to learn fine-grained action grounding across dialogue turns. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Before proceeding with full-scale Phase 1 training, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to determine optimal training configurations.

We experimented with different image sizes and coordinate representation systems to identify the optimal configuration for SmolVLM2:.

Some SOTA GUI VLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL) appear also to use a different normalized range (0–1000), which was not tested in this experiment.

Table 1: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (400k samples, aguvis-stage-1). Higher is better.

Industry observers note that as demonstrated in our benchmark results, SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct base initially achieved 0% performance on perception benchmarks like ScreenSpot-v2. This complete lack of grounding capability provided us with a clean slate to evaluate the effectiveness of our training methodology.

From our experiments, we determined that:.

Using the optimal configuration (1152px resolution with normalized coordinates), we trained for 2 epochs on the smolagents/aguvis-stage-1 dataset. The results were remarkable, +41% improvement over baseline on ScreenSpot-v2.

This dramatic improvement demonstrates that our Phase 1 training successfully instilled fundamental grounding capabilities in the model, enabling it to understand and locate visual elements within screenshots.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

Whereas Phase 1 provided grounding capabilities, Phase 2 targets agentic reasoning, the ability to deliberate and initiative before acting. This stage transforms the model from a reactive system identifying GUI elements into a proactive agent capable of executing complex, multi-step interactions.

Phase 2 uses the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 dataset, which introduces agentic scenarios:.

Explicit reasoning about upcoming actions.

Context consistency across multiple interaction steps.

High-level instructions require multi-step, low-level actions.

For example, the smolagents/aguvis-stage-2 chat message is like this:.

Each sample links a screenshot with a system/user/assistant turn. During fine-tuning, the data collator masks everything except the assistant’s answers when computing the loss.

Sources indicate that starting from the Phase 1 checkpoint (1152 px resolution, normalized coordinates), we fine-tuned the model for two epochs on smolagents/aguvis-stage-2. The accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 increased from 41% to 61%, indicating that explicit reasoning improves GUI grounding performance.

Table 2: Baseline on HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct after Phase 1 finetuning (2 epochs, aguvis-stage-1).

All training code, data processing pipelines, datasets and model are open-source!

Recent findings suggest that our experiments demonstrate that high-quality, reasoning-oriented data can substantially improve GUI grounding, even for small VLMs, using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Beyond raw performance gains, these results show that the GUI grounding capabilities are largely determined by the quality of the data. Carefully curated datasets teach models the structure and semantics of user interfaces, providing the grounding needed for accurate action prediction.

To support the development of GUI agents, we’re open-sourcing everything: our complete pipeline, datasets, and trained model. You can reproduce our results, experiment with different models and architectures, or adapt our approach to new domains. The future of agentic AI depends on researchers like you pushing these boundaries further!

In a recent development, while SFT excels at supervised tasks, emerging methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) help develop stronger reasoning capabilities and enable real-time adaptation. These advances point toward a fresh generation of GUI agents that learn and improve through interaction rather than relying solely on static datasets.

Let’s build the future of GUI agents together 🤗.

Sources indicate that we released swift-transformers two years ago (!) with the goal to support Apple developers and help them integrate local LLMs in their apps. A lot has changed since then (MLX and chat templates did not exist!), and we’ve learned how the community is actually using the library.

Industry observers note that we want to double down on the use cases that provide most benefits to the community, and lay out the foundations for the future. Spoiler alert: after this release, we’ll focus a lot on MLX and agentic use cases 🚀.

swift-transformers is a Swift library that aims to reduce the friction for developers that want to work with local models on Apple Silicon platforms, including iPhones. It includes the missing pieces that are not provided by Core ML or MLX alone, but that are required to work with local inference. Namely, it provides the following components:.

Most of the time people use the Tokenizers or Hub modules, and frequently both. Some notable projects that rely on swift-transformers include:.

Version 1.0 signals stability in the package. Developers are building apps on swift-transformers, and this first major release recognizes those use cases and brings the version number in line with that reality. It also provides the foundation on which to iterate with the community to build the next set of features. These are some of our preferred updates:.

Recent findings suggest that version 1.0 comes with breaking API changes. However, we don’t expect major problems if you are a user of Tokenizers or Hub. If you use the Core ML components of the library, please get in touch so we can support you during transition. We’ll prepare a migration guide and add it to the documentation.

Here's how to use Tokenizers to format tool calling input for an LLM:.

For additional examples, please check this section in the README and the Examples folder.

Sources indicate that honestly, we don’t know. We do know that we are super interested in exploring MLX, because that’s usually the current go-to approach for developers getting started with ML in native apps, and we want to help make the experience as seamless as possible. We are thinking along the lines of better integration with mlx-swift-examples for LLMs and VLMs, potentially through pre-processing and post-processing operations that developers encounter frequently.

It has been revealed that we are also extremely excited about agentic use in general and MCP in particular. We think that exposure of system resources to local workflows would be 🚀.

If you want to follow along in this journey or want to share your ideas, please contact us through our social networks or the repo.

We are immensely grateful to all the contributors and owners of the library for your help and feedback. We love you all, and can't wait to continue working with you to shape the future of on-device generation! ❤️.

Many thanks to the Hugging Face team for the recognition and for pushing the Swift ecosystem forward. It’s been an honor to contribute Swift Jinja to the community, and I look forward to building the future together!♥️♥️♥️.

How AIClaw 3.12.13 Loads Selected Skills Before the First Model Request

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (354 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A skill catalog is useful when the agent needs to discover a workflow.
  • AIClaw v3.12.13 gives an explicit selection a different path.
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine a mounted skill named release-check and a request like “$release-check summarize these changes.” The relevant instructions can shape the model's first response or tool choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A skill catalog is useful when the agent needs to discover a workflow. The timing matters when the user already picked one. If the instructions arrive through a tool call, the first model request still has to decide to make that call from the catalog and the user's message alone.

AIClaw v3.12.13 gives an explicit selection a different path. This behavior ships in the tagged release, and the source links below point to that version.

Recent findings suggest that imagine a mounted skill named release-check and a request like “$release-check summarize these changes.” The relevant instructions can shape the model's first response or tool choice. There is no prerequisite load_skill round trip for the excerpt. If the user just asks for a summary, the model can discover an applicable skill from the catalog and call load_skill as needed.

The kernel matches complete $skill-name references against mounted skills. It appends the selected text to the outgoing request in memory. The stored user message keeps its original text. A retry after context compaction can still carry the selection, and the next turn starts with fresh selection state. See the request assembly and skill prompt code.

The catalog uses an estimated budget of up to 2,000 tokens, reduced to 2% of the configured context window when that yields a smaller budget. AIClaw shortens descriptions to retain more names. If names alone exceed the budget, it can omit entries. An exact reference to a mounted skill still works even if the catalog leaves it out.

Selected text has a separate limit of 8 KiB per skill excerpt and 32 KiB across selected blocks. An excerpt shortened by the byte limit directs the model to load_skill for more detail. These are prompt assembly limits. The catalog uses a token estimate, and supplying instructions gives no guarantee that a model will follow them.

The kernel regressions inspect requests captured by a test model. They cover first-request inclusion, turn scoping, a compaction retry, catalog limits, and UTF-8 truncation. Those checks establish what the kernel sends. They do not measure live-model instruction following, latency, or provider token usage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

高品質で多様なトレーニングデータなしに、日本文化を真に理解するAIを構築することはこれまでほぼ不可能でした。これを変えるため、NVIDIAは、日本の人口統計、地理的分布、文化的特性に沿ったペルソナを含む初のオープン合成データセット、Nemotron-Personas-Japan を公開しました。CC BY 4.0 ライセンスのもと提供される本データセットは、機微な個人データに依存することなく日本社会を反映した AI システム構築のための、プライバシー保護と規制対応を両立した基盤を提供します。.

NVIDIA のエンタープライズ向け合成データ生成システム、NeMo Data Designer を用いて作成されたNemotron-Personas-Japan は、すでに広く利用されている US Personas データセットの成功を機に日本版として開発されました。本リリースは、各国・地域におけるソブリン AI 開発を支援する合成ペルソナデータセットとデータ構築方法のグローバルコレクションの第一弾です。.

本データセットは、Nemotron モデルをはじめとするオープンソースの 大規模言語モデル(LLM) とシームレスに連携するよう設計されており、企業向けチャットボットから各種ドメインの AI エージェントに至るまで、日本語 AI アプリケーション向けのファインチューンを容易に行えるようになっています。.

NVIDIAの合成データ生成用マイクロサービスである NeMo Data Designer を用いて構築されています。この複合AIシステムは、複雑な Jinja テンプレート、Pydantic による検証、構造化出力、自動リトライ、および複数の生成バックエンドのサポートを可能にします。これらは、このような大規模な合成データセットの生成に必要なツール群です。さらに、以下のモデルも活用しています。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan は、日本の公的な人口統計および労働統計に整合するよう設計されると同時に、AI トレーニングにおいて重要な以下の点を考慮して生成されました：.

このデータセットには、個人を特定できる情報（PII）は一切含まれていません。年齢、名前、職業などは公的な統計データの分布に基づいていますが、存命・故人問わず、実在の人物と結びつくことはありません。全てのペルソナは完全に人工的に生成されているため、実際の文化的パターンを保ちながらも、個人のプライバシーを損なうことなくトレーニングに利用できます。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japanは、日本のソブリン AI システムを開発する日本のモデル開発者向けに設計されています。現在、LLM開発者が使用する訓練データのほとんどは英語であり、日本やインドなど各地域の開発者は、母国語で高品質なデータを入手するのに苦労しています。.

本データセットを含め、NVIDIA の Nemotron-Personas の一連の取り組みは、こうした課題を直接解決するものです。地域固有のニュアンスを捉えつつ、開発者が地域固有の言語で多様かつ複雑なデータを生成できるようサポートします。データセットは国勢調査データ、日本人の命名規則、文化的特徴など地域のコンテキストに基づき、すべて母語で生成しています。.

そのため、日本で自分たちのモデルの採用を拡大し、日本の文化的コンテキストを理解したい すべての AI モデルの開発者の方々のお役に立てれば幸いです。.

本データセットに含まれる合成ペルソナを以下のようなことに活用できます：.

AI 開発には、実世界の人々を反映した多様で高品質な訓練データへのアクセスが長らく課題でした。企業向け AI の開発はプライベートデータが主流となっており、研究者、スタートアップ、そして特に利用可能なデータが少ない地域のAI開発者にとって障壁となっていました。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan を CC BY 4.0 のもとで公開することで、企業レベルの高品質な合成データへのアクセスを可能とし、従来のコスト、プライバシーの懸念、地理的な制約といった障壁なしに、文化的背景を正確に反映した AI システムを誰でも構築できるようになりました。.

以下のコマンドで本データセットをダウンロードできます。日本文化と言語を真に理解する AIの開発にお役立てください。.

日本でソブリン AI を開発するモデル開発者から、より広範な地域での利用を目指すグローバルな開発者まで、Nemotron-Personas-Japan データセットは、アプリケーションに必要な本格的かつプライバシーに配慮した基盤を提供します。.

Latest Update: OAuth Consent Phishing: How Malicious Apps Pass MFA and How to Shut Them Down in Entra ID

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, OAuth consent phishing never asks for a password.
  • According to recent reports, this guide covers how the attack works at the protocol level, the Entra ID consent settings that close it, a KQL detection you can deploy today, and the exact commands to clean up after a successful grant.
  • According to recent reports, the attacker's app is just an ordinary registration with a redirect URI they control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, OAuth consent phishing never asks for a password. The attacker registers a multi-tenant application, sends the victim a link to the real login.microsoftonline.com authorize URL, and waits for the user to click Accept. Every step the victim sees is genuine, including MFA, which is why this attack class keeps working against organisations that think they are covered by phishing-resistant authentication. What matters is not who the user is, but what they just authorised an unknown app to do.

According to recent reports, this guide covers how the attack works at the protocol level, the Entra ID consent settings that close it, a KQL detection you can deploy today, and the exact commands to clean up after a successful grant. For the related token-theft pattern that abuses RFC 8628 instead of the authorization code flow, see OAuth Device Code Flow Security.

According to recent reports, the attacker's app is just an ordinary registration with a redirect URI they control. The lure is a standard authorization request:.

Industry observers note that from then on the attacker calls Microsoft Graph as the app. The grant is independent of the user's password and sessions, so a password reset does not remove it. This is the same refresh-token persistence problem seen in MFA bypass attacks, except here Microsoft itself issued the token to the attacker's client at the user's request.

Variants you will see in incident reports:.

Microsoft documents three user consent settings in Entra ID: do not allow user consent, allow consent only for apps from verified publishers requesting low-impact permissions, or let Microsoft manage your consent settings (the default for newly introduced tenants, backed by the microsoft-user-default-recommended policy). Check which one your tenant is on before assuming you are protected.

Read the current assignment with Microsoft Graph PowerShell:.

Sources indicate that if this returns ManagePermissionGrantsForSelf.microsoft-user-default-legacy, users can consent to almost anything that does not require admin consent. Move to a stricter setting.

This is the strongest control and fits regulated tenants. Pair it with the admin consent workflow below, otherwise users hit a dead end and look for workarounds.

Note the weakness: it depends on the verified-publisher signal, and the permission classification (which scopes count as low impact) is something you must review rather than assume. Mail.Read should never be classified low-impact in a tenant that cares about mailbox confidentiality.

In the Entra admin center go to Enterprise applications > Consent and permissions > Admin consent settings and set Consumers can request admin consent to apps they are unable to consent to to Yes, then pick reviewers. Users get a request button on the consent prompt instead of a block, and reviewers see the app, publisher and exact scopes before approving. Make sure reviewers know to decline anything requesting offline_access plus mail or file scopes from an unverified publisher.

Microsoft's risk-based step-up consent turns a user consent request that Microsoft flags as risky into a requirement for admin consent. It only changes behaviour when user consent is enabled, and the BlockUserConsentForRiskyApps setting is controlled through the Graph PowerShell beta module with the Privileged Role Administrator role. Treat it as a useful extra layer, not a substitute for restricting consent: the flag is advisory and attackers iterate until their app is not flagged.

Entra ID writes a Consent to application audit event each time a user or admin grants consent. Forward the AuditLogs table to Microsoft Sentinel (or Log Analytics) and run:.

It has been revealed that property positions in modifiedProperties vary by event shape, so run this once against a known consent in your tenant and adjust the index before turning it into an alert. Elastic's prebuilt rule uses the same event with a new-terms approach (first time a user and application pair is seen in the recent window), which keeps a campaign hitting many customers visible because each pair alerts separately.

In a recent development, do not wait for an alert. List every delegated grant in the tenant and review it:.

ConsentType of AllPrincipals means an admin granted it for the whole tenant, which deserves the most scrutiny. Principal means a single user consented. Resolve ClientId to the service principal with Get-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId and check the publisher, creation date and sign-in activity. Apps nobody on your team can explain are candidates for removal.

Industry observers note that A password reset alone leaves the attacker's refresh token valid. Run all four steps:.

Recent findings suggest that the equivalent REST call for step 1 is DELETE https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants/{id}. After cleanup, search the mailbox for inbox rules and forwarding the attacker may have created while they had Mail.ReadWrite, and review what the app read through the unified audit log so you can decide on disclosure.

Sources indicate that consent phishing succeeds because identity teams spend their effort on authentication strength and treat authorisation as a user decision. Passkeys and number matching do nothing here: the user authenticated correctly and then authorised the wrong party. The durable fix is making consent an administrative decision for anything beyond trivial scopes, and watching the audit log for the exceptions. If your org also exposes OAuth-based integrations to AI agents, the same principle applies to what those agents may be granted; see MCP OAuth 2.1 authentication and the OAuth 2.1 security best practices guide. To inspect the tokens an app receives during a test, use the JWT Decoder.

Latest Update: VibeGame: Exploring Vibe Coding Games

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that people are trying to vibe code games.
  • I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.
  • Industry observers note that first, what is vibe coding?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that people are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

Industry observers note that first, what is vibe coding? It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".

However, since then, it's used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just "using AI when coding" to "not thinking about the code at all". In this blog post, I'll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what's going on under the hood, but doesn't necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

According to recent reports, earlier I mentioned that "as the project grows, things begin to fall apart". This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very quickly.

To address this concern, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

Sources indicate that I couldn't find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn't rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:.

Recent findings suggest that anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model's context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Industry observers note that beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

Sources indicate that the official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

In a recent development, roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it's in-house at Roblox.

Recent findings suggest that the unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

Unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

This approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:.

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

Sources indicate that this will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

In a recent development, here's the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

However, there are still some major caveats:.

So, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot "make me a game" approach, it doesn't work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires people to understand the engine's capabilities and limitations.

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:.

Then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

Industry observers note that the engine is currently very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

It has been revealed that it's also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We're also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

Follow me to keep up with what's going on in the space!

Industry observers note that thanks for the post ! If you have feedback or feature requests the Roblox MCP server, feel free to submit problems on the project page:.

https://github.com/Roblox/studio-rust-mcp-server.

Also it is open source, so you can hack on it and add more context management tools here:https://github.com/Roblox/studio-rust-mcp-server/tree/main/plugin/src/Tools.

This is very cool! A mini-engine with API designed for LLMs may be able to supercharge game development.

https://urlquery.net/report/08590583-4f70-4098-b269-48e3c8d25f4f.

Here is a platform for vibe game development; https://exekite.com/.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (481 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Why I'm Moving My C++ Networking Library From C++26 to C++17

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (481 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I started developing LightnerX, I decided to use C++26 modules.
  • At the time, it seemed like a reasonable choice.
  • Well, there's one problem: not everyone is using C++26.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I started developing LightnerX, I decided to use C++26 modules.

At the time, it seemed like a reasonable choice. I was building a new library, so why not use the latest features available?

Well, there's one problem: not everyone is using C++26.

And when you're developing an open-source library that other people are supposed to integrate into their projects, compatibility matters. What is LightnerX?

LightnerX is an open-source C++ networking library I've been developing for multiplayer games.

It originally started as part of my own game project, but eventually became a standalone library.

It uses Valve's GameNetworkingSockets as its transport layer and implements INER, a communication model I designed around four message types:.

LightnerX also provides connection management, message interpretation, callbacks, and message batching.

Recent findings suggest that the idea is to provide a relatively small networking library that developers can integrate into their own games without adopting an entire networking framework. The compatibility problem.

My original implementation relied on C++26 modules and newer standard library features.

That worked for my development environment, but it also introduced requirements that many existing projects might not satisfy.

For example, someone developing a game with a C++17 codebase would need to deal with those requirements just to integrate LightnerX.

So I started working on a C++17 migration. What needs to change?

This isn't just about changing the CMake standard from 26 to 17.

The migration involves several changes:.

The original library uses .cppm files and module imports.

The C++17 version needs conventional .hpp and .cpp files, with the appropriate includes and declarations.

Some of the original implementation relies on features such as std::span and std::expected.

Since these aren't available in C++17, I'm implementing compatible alternatives within the LightnerX namespace.

This is probably the most vital part.

I don't want to redesign the library during the migration.

The objective is to preserve its behavior and functionality while making the implementation compatible with an older C++ standard.

That means reviewing the API, testing edge cases, and checking that the migration doesn't introduce regressions. Why C++17?

I considered other standards, but C++17 felt like a reasonable compatibility target.

It's modern enough for the architecture I'm using while allowing developers with older C++ projects to integrate the library more easily.

Recent findings suggest that and honestly, I would rather spend time improving the networking library than require people to change their entire toolchain to try it. What's next?

The C++17 migration is part of my effort to make LightnerX more practical for other developers.

I'm also working on testing, documentation, and examples that demonstrate how to use the library in actual applications.

If you're interested in multiplayer networking, C++, or open-source game development, I'd appreciate any feedback.

I'm particularly curious about one thing:.

When choosing a C++ library for your own project, how much does the minimum required C++ standard influence your decision?
