Latest Update: De-identifying medical records with MedGemma so that no one sees the raw data: a look at a live deployment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JointSpace is a physical therapy clinic in Dubai.
  • Yma Health solved this with us, and it's now in production with two customers: the clinic and Simplex Himes, a certified EHR provider in the UAE.
  • The regulator is the Dubai Health Authority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Nukri Basharuli and George Zhgenti.

JointSpace is a physical therapy clinic in Dubai. It wanted a model that could read a patient's full rehab history — comorbidities, progress notes, therapist comments — and help strategy treatment. A hosted API was off the table: their clinical director put it plainly, sending data to external APIs was a non-starter. Running a model of the right quality in-house wasn't realistic either.

Yma Health solved this with us, and it's now in production with two customers: the clinic and Simplex Himes, a certified EHR provider in the UAE. Below is how it works, a code pattern you can adapt, and how this maps to HIPAA and GDPR if you're not in Dubai.

The regulator is the Dubai Health Authority. DHA treats data as personal unless both direct identifiers and quasi-identifiers are removed. Stripping the name and the Emirates ID number doesn't get you there. Age plus neighborhood plus a rare diagnosis plus an employer often points to exactly one person.

Sources indicate that rules and regexes catch direct identifiers but miss context. They won't flag "the only commercial pilot among the clinic's patients." A model will. So Yma gave the de-identification job to Google's MedGemma 27B, a multimodal model that reads both the text of a record and its images.

In a recent development, that creates a different problem. To de-identify a record, the model first has to read it raw, so the raw record has to reach wherever the model runs.

Sources indicate that yma calls its layer a "VPN for healthcare." It's middleware that runs on Super Protocol inside attested confidential environments. The flow:.

None of the participants sees the raw records: not Simplex, not Yma, not Super, not Nebius, not the preprocessing provider. No changes were made to the certified EHR systems, and the clinics kept their existing workflows.

The snippets below are our own example. They follow the same pattern as the production setup, but they aren't Yma's code. MedGemma runs here as a dedicated deployment inside a confidential environment, not as a model from the shared Router catalog. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so the client code is the same as in our previous post on Confidential Router:.

Recent findings suggest that A model's output is probabilistic, so it doesn't get the final say. A deterministic check runs after it, and that check decides whether a record leaves:.

Where this runs matters. deidentify, release_ok and the raw record all live inside the confidential environment. If the model misses something and the check catches it, the raw record goes nowhere: it stays inside and gets flagged for review. In a conventional setup, a de-identification miss means the operator of the machine running the model has already had access to raw PHI.

HIPAA gives you two routes to de-identification. Safe Harbor means removing 18 listed identifier types. Expert Determination means a qualified expert concludes the re-identification risk is very small. DHA's approach to quasi-identifiers is closer to the second. An LLM step doesn't make data de-identified under HIPAA on its own; your expert and your method do.

Sources indicate that there's a second piece. While raw records are being processed inside the environment, they're PHI. Since 2016, HHS guidance has been clear that a cloud provider is a business associate even if it stores only encrypted ePHI and has no key. Confidential computing doesn't remove the need for a BAA. What it does is shrink the set of people who can technically see the data, and make that verifiable. Super signs BAAs.

Under GDPR, pseudonymized data is still personal data. Only truly anonymous data falls outside the regulation (Recital 26), and the bar is high — the same quasi-identifier logic DHA uses. Processing raw records is processing health data, a special category under Article 9. You'll need a DPA with each processor and most likely a DPIA. Attestation helps you show technical measures under Article 32: you have cryptographic proof of which code processed the data and that the operator couldn't access it.

As reported by Yma and its customers:.

Sergei Savvov, Yma's co-founder and CTO, claims they previously had to write extensive custom anonymization code; MedGemma now does that work inside the secure environment. Google features the project in its Health AI Developer Foundations showcase.

Full case study: superprotocol.com/case-studies/yma.

A compound AI approach to Indian personas grounded in real-world distributions.

India represents one of the world's largest AI opportunities — with over 700 million internet people, a multitude of languages, and a rapidly growing developer ecosystem. Yet, most open datasets reflect Western norms and English-only contexts, creating a data gap that limits AI adoption in India's multilingual, multi-script environment.

According to recent reports, today, we're releasing Nemotron-Personas-India, the first open synthetic dataset of Indic personas aligned to India's real-world demographic, geographic, and cultural distributions. Licensed under CC BY 4.0, this dataset offers a privacy-preserving, regulation-ready foundation for scaling AI systems that reflect Indian society—without relying on sensitive personal data.

Built with NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's enterprise-grade synthetic data generation microservice, Nemotron-Personas-India extends our global collection of Sovereign AI datasets. It builds on the success of our US and Japan persona datasets and includes newly introduced features designed specifically for India's culturally rich landscape.

This dataset integrates seamlessly with Nemotron models and other open-source LLMs, making it easy to fine-tune AI systems for Indian use cases—from multilingual chatbots to culturally-grounded specialized copilots.

This release complements our earlier suite of Hindi evaluation datasets — including ChatRAG-Hi, IFEval-Hi, MT-Bench-Hi, GSM8K-Hi, and BFCL-Hi — supporting a complete pipeline from synthetic data generation to rigorous model evaluation for Indian AI systems.

Produced using NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's microservice for synthetic data generation. This compound AI system enables generation with complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and supports multiple generation backends – the necessary tooling to scale a synthetic dataset of this size. We also leveraged the following models:.

This dataset was aligned to India’s official demographic distributions from the 2011 Census and expanded to include attributes essential for trustworthy AI training:.

Recent findings suggest that no real names. No re-identification risk.

It has been revealed that all personas are fully synthetic. While grounded in real-world distributions from the 2011 Census and Parsed Indian Electoral Rolls data, no data is tied to any living or deceased individual. This ensures developers can safely train AI systems without privacy risks or regulatory barriers.

Built for India, Ready for the World.

Nemotron‑Personas‑India is designed for developers building Sovereign AI systems for the Indian market, as well as global teams looking to adapt models to India’s unique linguistic, cultural, and social context.

Most open datasets today reflect English-speaking, Western norms—limiting AI performance in India’s multilingual, multi-script, and demographically complex environments.

With Nemotron‑Personas‑India, teams can:.

Recent findings suggest that india's 1.4 billion people speak hundreds of languages and live across vast cultural, economic, and geographic divides. India's National AI Portal estimates over 7,000 AI startups and research institutions are working to build locally relevant AI systems, and the Digital India initiative and government programs like IndiaAI are accelerating adoption.

It has been revealed that but progress is constrained by a fundamental gap: high-quality, culturally grounded training data that reflects India's demographic reality. Without representative datasets, AI systems struggle with code-switching between English and Hindi, fail to understand regional occupational categories, and miss cultural context essential for trust and adoption.

The dataset improves diversity of synthetically-generated data, mitigates biases, and prevents model collapse (degradation caused by uncurated training on another model's outputs) by reflecting India's real geographic and demographic distributions.

Nemotron-Personas-India supports Indian model builders in developing Sovereign AI systems that incorporate vital region-specific demographics and cultural context.

Want to build AI systems that understand India's culture, languages, and people?

Whether you're an Indian model builder developing Sovereign AI or a global developer seeking better regional adoption, Nemotron-Personas-India provides the authentic, privacy-safe foundation your applications need.

Coding agents burn tokens on repeated file reads. Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex scan the same functions over and over because they lack persistent memory of codebase structure. CodeGraph solves this by maintaining a live semantic graph that agents query instead of scanning files.

The project sits at 78K+ GitHub stars and trending #11 in TypeScript. It runs 100% local with a Rust-powered kernel that watches file changes and incrementally updates the graph. The MCP server exposes this graph as a tool boundary for agents.

Coding agents typically operate in two modes:.

This pattern wastes tokens and introduces latency. A 10,000-line monorepo might require 50+ file reads per agent session. Each read costs tokens and round-trip time.

In a recent development, codeGraph pre-indexes the codebase into a queryable graph. Agents ask "show me all functions that call authenticate" instead of reading 20 files to find them. The graph persists across sessions, so repeated queries cost nothing.

CodeGraph splits into two layers:.

In a recent development, rust kernel: Watches file system events, parses code into AST nodes, and updates the graph incrementally. When you edit a function, only that function's subgraph updates. Full re-indexing happens only on initial setup or major refactors.

MCP server: Exposes the graph as a tool boundary. Agents call structured queries like find_callers(function_name) or get_dependencies(module_path). The server translates these into graph traversals and returns results as JSON.

The kernel uses tree-sitter for parsing, which supports 40+ languages. Each language gets its own parser, but the graph schema is uniform: nodes represent symbols (functions, classes, variables), edges represent relationships (calls, imports, inheritance).

In a recent development, the graph lives in a local SQLite database. Schema looks like this:.

SQLite handles query speed well for graphs under 100K nodes. For larger monorepos, the kernel can export to a graph database like Neo4j, but most projects stay under the SQLite threshold.

Natural language queries: The server embeds a small LLM (Phi-3 or similar) that translates plain English into structured queries. Example: "What functions depend on the database connection?" becomes a graph traversal for all nodes with edges to the db_connection module.

Natural language queries add 50-200ms latency but reduce the need for agents to understand the graph schema.

Recent findings suggest that file watching uses platform-native APIs (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows). When a file changes:.

The kernel doesn't parse Python's internal structure from TypeScript. It just records the dependency. When an agent queries "what depends on data_loader?", it sees fetchData in the results.

It has been revealed that codeGraph ships with MCP server configs for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others. The agent sees CodeGraph as a tool with these capabilities:.

#57482. Industry News: Four Ways to Help Newcomers Feel Like They Belong

Industry News: Four Ways to Help Newcomers Feel Like They Belong

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, liz Cahill was born and raised in Philadelphia.
  • It has been revealed that “I stated goodbye to everything I knew and loved in Philadelphia and came to the Bay.
  • Sources indicate that when she arrived, it hit her.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, liz Cahill was born and raised in Philadelphia. Her whole family is from Philadelphia, going back generations. One day, she was offered an internship in the Bay Area and decided to make the leap, despite not knowing anything about it or anyone there.

It has been revealed that “I stated goodbye to everything I knew and loved in Philadelphia and came to the Bay. Not knowing a soul.”.

Sources indicate that when she arrived, it hit her. “I was like, wow, I’m in a place that like, literally nobody knows me. So if I am dead in a ditch, like nobody will figure it out for a long time.”.

It has been revealed that this could have been a story of loneliness and disconnection, but it wasn’t, because someone took her under their wings—actually two strangers, her roommates Lauren and Deirdre. “They took me in and welcomed me and brought me into their whole social world, which showed me so much love.”.

This isn’t the experience for most people. Darilys Matos Acevedo grew up in Puerto Rico. “In Puerto Rico, a stranger talks to you all the time. If you went down the street and you talked to somebody, if you made eye contact . . . you had to smile at them or you noted good morning or good afternoon.”.

Then she moved to Boston for graduate school. “I had never even visited the place. I knew nobody here.” And where she got smiles and small talk in Puerto Rico, in Boston she “got glares.” “And I’m like, oh, OK. You don’t do any of that here.” It was painful and created a large void in her life.

In a recent development, as Darilys talked to other Latinos in Boston, she assumed “I’m the only one who feels this way, but I wasn’t. There was like a whole group of people that felt like that.”.

Their stories are different, but they reveal the same truth.

Industry observers note that moving doesn’t simply change where we live. It interrupts the invisible web of relationships that makes everyday life feel familiar, that makes us feel like we belong. And the majority of the 13 million American adults who move each year experience this.

Industry observers note that at the US Chamber of Connection, our recent study on social connection in America explored the impact of life transitions on social connection. It found that 40% of people navigating a relocation struggle with social connection, and they report 35% more barriers to connection compared to everyone else. Two of the most common barriers are not knowing where to start and not wanting to go out alone.

Industry observers note that the impact is lasting, as someone shared with us. “Two years ago, I was going on a vacation, and I could not find ONE neighbor to water my plants while I was away. I had lived in this building on and off for over 15 years. I was mortified. How could it be that I had nobody in my building to help with such a small task?”.

Moving ranks among the most stressful life events a person can experience, on par with divorce and job loss. But the stress isn’t just logistical; it’s psychological. Moving severs the informal ties and daily routines that quietly anchor our sense of who we are and where we belong. The result is a predictable but rarely named experience: not just loneliness, but identity dislocation. The question isn’t only “who do I know here?” but “who am I here?”.

This month, we're teaming up with the US Chamber of Connection for Welcome Week. Together, we're mobilizing communities, neighborhoods, and organizations nationwide to do one simple thing this September: open the door to a upcoming friend. Make a pledge to invite someone in and help us reach our goal to make 100,000 people feel welcomed!

In a recent development, to understand the scale of that loss, consider what a typical adult social network requires to build: roughly 200 hours to develop a close friend, 90 hours for a friend, and five hours of repeated interaction for each of the weak ties (neighbors, familiar faces, community contacts) that make daily life feel anchored. A typical adult carries around 1,300 hours of accumulated relationship time. When you move, you leave all of it behind and start from zero.

This is also, paradoxically, what makes the first year after a move one of the most powerful windows for connection. Disruption breaks old habits and makes people unusually open to forming new ones, a phenomenon researchers call the habit discontinuity effect. People who have just moved are more likely to join things, try things, and reach out than they were six months earlier at home.

Sources indicate that what closes that window isn’t lack of desire. Research by Nicholas Epley at the University of Chicago finds that people systematically underestimate how much strangers want to connect and overestimate how awkward the attempt will be. Both the newcomer and the potential neighbor hold back, each assuming the other isn’t interested. Both tend to be wrong.

Industry observers note that and the effects of getting it right last longer than most people expect. Vanessa Elias, the founder of Block Party USA, shared with us the story of a neighbor who brought her family a pie when she moved in as a six year old. She remembers her name, Mrs. Fisher, decades later.

Recent findings suggest that what would happen if welcoming became a civic practice instead of an individual virtue? This year, the US Chamber of Connection recruited over 250 people across 25 states to run creative experiments that aimed to help others feel more welcome in their neighborhoods. They were trained on the science of connection and worked together across the country to support each other. We call them the Welcome Committee.

For many of the volunteers, they signed up because they had an experience like Liz. One shared that “when we arrived to our new town we felt welcomed, surprised, and alive through these touches, and wanted to build more.” Or as another volunteer explained, “people are still welcoming me and I still feel at home here. So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I wanna create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”.

It has been revealed that for others, it came from an experience more akin to Darilys’s. “I would have loved to find this kind of thing when I moved,” shared one early volunteer. “I’ve been in my neighborhood and city since 2019 and have yet to make close friends in the neighborhood or city where I live. It feels scary and uncomfortable to get out there. But I’m realizing the huge impact of not having close friends. I’m ready to make the effort. Because if I’m feeling this way, I can’t be the only one.”.

In a recent development, they each began by inviting a neighbor for a conversation. They shared their stories of their neighborhoods growing up. Dreamed about the ideal neighborhood together. Explored the Six Points of Connection, a clear and actionable checklist for individuals and leaders to define and strengthen social bonds. And then they explored how they might together make the neighborhood more connected.

Industry observers note that they ran some creative experiments. Lindsay turned their suburban garage door into a community message board. Kaitlin created a traveling tin of homemade baked goods that moves neighbor to neighbor down the street, each recipient required to bake something and pass it on to someone latest. Sarah hosted a gathering for other people named Sara(h) in her town. Courtney started flyering the neighborhood to organize a dog gathering in someone’s backyard. Nithya left a flower and a handwritten note for each of the five nearest neighbors inviting them to coffee.

According to recent reports, many of the volunteers nostalgically tried things they remembered from their childhood or had seen in a movie. Kate moved an iron chair and table to her front step and started having her morning coffee there facing the street. Jon made lemonade with his kids and set out donuts for anyone walking by. Chet started introducing himself on his daily dog walks. Anne organized a multi-household yard sale across eight houses. And many of them hosted potlucks and block parties.

They all expressed knowing “how meaningful it can be to walk into a upcoming space and find someone who is genuinely glad you are there.” And they wanted to make people feel that way.

Industry observers note that as the volunteers conducted their experiments, they began to share their findings. They mirrored much of what we have learned from social scientists over the last 50 years. Four themes emerged that help to inform how we can all do more to help new residents, and any neighbor, feel more welcomed.

According to recent reports, 1. The first step is the most key. Stop playing “invite chicken.” Many of our volunteers shared a version of the same experience: sitting at home hoping someone would call and invite them to hang out, attend an event, or even just watch Netflix together. They assumed that the people they wanted to call were probably busy or uninterested. Those people were likely sitting at home thinking the same thing. Nobody called. Everyone stayed alone.

Call it invite chicken: a standoff where everyone loses despite everyone wanting the same thing. The barrier isn’t reality; it’s anticipation. Someone just has to go first.

Industry observers note that and sometimes, when we do break the game of chicken, we don’t get the response we wanted. When Hazel hosted her first neighborhood coffee gathering, one neighbor texted that he was too nervous to come. She didn’t give up. She texted back encouraging him. He came. At one of Elizabeth’s gatherings in San Diego, a man had been dragged along by his wife, who promised they’d stay just five minutes. He was the last to leave.

Recent findings suggest that we are poor forecasters of our own social experiences. People overweight the discomfort of initiation and underweight the pleasure of connection. The host who sends the follow-up text, the wife who insists on five minutes, isn’t being pushy. They’re correcting for a cognitive error the reluctant person can’t see from the inside.

Industry observers note that 2. We are more motivated working together. Partner with someone. Erin hosted a neighborhood gathering in Newly introduced York City and reflected afterward on what she’d do differently. Her top lesson: “I appreciated the help I did get from neighbors and wished I’d had a co-planner to share more of the work with.”.

In a recent development, this is consistent with what research finds: People are significantly more likely to initiate and sustain kind and helpful behavior when they’re doing it alongside someone else. A partner doesn’t just make the work easier; they make follow-through more likely, because the social cost of backing out now involves someone else. Several Welcome Committee volunteers named the US Chamber of Connection cohort itself as the thing that got them out the door. Not the training, not the tools, but the fact that others were doing it, too.

According to recent reports, 3. We gain comfort with repeat exposure. Build a rhythm. Hansen has been hosting a monthly porch gathering (coffee, bagels, same spot) for two years. Recently, he watched neighbors spontaneously make intends to go cycling together and quietly organize to look out for a boy on the street whose father is dying of cancer. Neither of those things was planned. They happened because the same people had been attending his events and they had built comfort with each other. Hansen didn’t suggest they help the boy but had created the environment for it to be possible.

Sources indicate that research finds that repeated contact with the same faces makes us like and trust them more, independent of what’s remarked. Those repeated encounters build weak ties, which are how people find help in a crisis, how trust spreads beyond close friends, how a community starts to look out for itself. The first gathering gets you in the door. Showing up again is what builds the neighborhood.

Sources indicate that what these moments share is spontaneity and clarity of intent. Research finds that unexpected gestures create a positive disruption that formal invitations don’t. They bypass the social calculation people run when a stranger approaches, and they signal warmth without asking for anything back. Research finds that being noticed is the precondition for feeling like you belong.

Sources indicate that and having a clear role removes the ambiguity that makes first moves feel risky. When Annie said “I’m a Welcome Committee member,” her motives were transparent before she said another word. You don’t need a blueprint. You need to look up.

Giving to others produces more sustained well-being than spending on yourself. The helper’s high is real. Welcoming a newcomer isn’t just a form of service; it’s one of the highest-return social investments you can make.

Liz knows this firsthand. The woman who arrived in the Bay Area not knowing a soul, wondering if anyone would notice if she disappeared, is now the person who creates spaces for others to land. “People here took a chance on me,” she claims. “So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I want to create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”.

All friendships begin the same way: by talking to strangers. Someone just has to go first. Years later, Liz became the person who notices.

Aaron Hurst is a pioneer social entrepreneur and CEO focused on rebuilding human connection to strengthen communities. He founded the U.S. Chamber of Connection to address the national decline in social ties and trust. Previously, he founded the Taproot Foundation, sparking a $15B pro bono service movement, and led Imperative, which developed purpose profiling tools used by over 200 companies. He’s also co-founder of Board.Dev, connecting tech leaders to nonprofit boards. Author of The Purpose Economy, Aaron’s work has shaped the purpose movement in business and been featured in The Upcoming York Times, Bloomberg, and SSIR. He lives in Seattle with his family.

Leaked or generated? Notes on Reuters' Muse report and the records that could tell

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on 18 November 2026 Reuters reported on Muse, the personal AI agent Meta debuted in September.
  • Industry observers note that meta notes users can see an audit trail of Muse's past and planned actions.
  • These are engineering notes we draw from the case, not findings in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on 18 November 2026 Reuters reported on Muse, the personal AI agent Meta debuted in September. Reuters had reviewed more than two dozen internal posts in which Meta employees described unwanted actions by the agent, and reproduced one of them with staff from Signal and the AI Now Institute. At VSO we check incident reports against sources before writing about them; our record for this one is V1118MUSE. This post pulls out what it means for people who build agents that act on a user's device and accounts.

Industry observers note that meta notes users can see an audit trail of Muse's past and planned actions. The outside account, though, rests on employees' posts and a replication. The open question, leaked or generated, can be answered only from records the operator holds.

These are engineering notes we draw from the case, not findings in the report.

According to recent reports, the reported reads did not go through the integration layer that users manage; they went through an operating-system permission. If your harness logs only calls through your own connectors, an agent that reaches data another way leaves no trace in your trail.

Sources indicate that note: Log reads at the point where content enters the agent's context, whatever the path, and record the path itself (connector, notification listener, accessibility API, screenshot). An entry that says "read Signal notification via notification-listener permission" answers a question that "context updated" does not.

Recent findings suggest that "Was this another user's data?" is a question about the inputs present when an output was generated. If your records hold only outputs, you cannot answer it, and neither can anyone you show them to.

Industry observers note that note: For each generated message or action, record references to the inputs in context (by content hash and source, not by copying the content), linked to the output by a shared trace identifier. Then a misdirected message can be traced back: either another account's record appears among its inputs or it does not.

A bank balance retrieved from an account and a bank balance the model produced look the same in an output log.

Recent findings suggest that note: Tag numbers, names and account details in outputs with their origin: retrieved from a named source, or generated. It is cheap at write time and impossible to reconstruct later.

According to recent reports, an in-app audit trail helps users. It does not let anyone else check that what is shown is complete and unaltered.

Industry observers note that note: If you want outsiders to be able to check, sign records as they are written, commit batches to something you do not control (a transparency log or timestamping service), and record how many events each batch should contain. Then omissions after commitment can be detected by someone other than you.

The content an agent reads through a notification is often exactly what should not be duplicated into logs.

Note: Record hashes and references, keep content in a store with its own access control, and proposal for erasing it.

According to recent reports, we develop VAP, a metaframework for making records of AI decisions and actions auditable and attributable after the fact. Note 4 is roughly what VAP v1.2 specifies: signed records, cryptographically verifiable order and membership, external anchoring at every conformance level, and a Completeness Invariant (INT-008) that makes omission after anchoring detectable at anchor granularity. The Traceability Layer requires that causal links between events can be expressed, which is the structure note 2 needs.

But VAP does not cover this case well, and we would rather say so:.

"does not warrant the correctness, fairness, or safety of the underlying AI decisions — only the integrity, completeness (at anchor granularity), and attributability of their records." (VAP v1.2 §1.6(c)).

Breaking: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions

📅 04 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A new study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain.
  • In a recent development, fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making.
  • It has been revealed that decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A new study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain. Researchers from the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) and Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin found that longer exhalations increased heart rate variability and made the brain more responsive to rewards, which was associated with bolder choices. The findings were published in Neuron.

In a recent development, fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making. Under pressure, people may become more cautious in an effort to avoid losses, whether they are making an investment, handling a tense workplace situation, or choosing a meal swiftly. Slower breathing and a calmer cardiovascular state, by contrast, may encourage a more positive assessment of potential outcomes and make people more willing to take risks.

How Breathing Connects the Body and Brain.

It has been revealed that decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain. The new research examined a broader possibility: that signals from other parts of the body can change brain activity and influence the choices people make.

Sources indicate that the study was led by Prof. Soyoung Q Park in collaboration with researchers from institutions including the Neuroscience Research Center at Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the German Naval Institute of Maritime Medicine.

"Our decisions are rarely determined solely by external information. Rather, our judgment emerges from the interplay between cognitive processes and our current bodily state. It was previously unknown how the conscious regulation of our body, for example through targeted breathing, could actively control our decision-making process. We wanted to create a physiological shift using a slow breathing pattern to change the quality of our decisions," explains Soyoung Q Park, head of the Department of Decision Neuroscience and Nutrition at DIfE, summarizing the research question.

Testing Whether Longer Exhales Change Decisions.

The researchers studied 41 healthy participants while they made risky choices under carefully controlled breathing conditions. Participants followed visual breathing instructions and either breathed at their normal individual pace or slowed their breathing while extending the exhalation phase (2:8 inhale-exhale ratio).

It has been revealed that as the participants completed a series of risk-related decisions, the research team measured several aspects of their physical and neurological responses. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to track brain activity, while breathing patterns, heart activity, skin conductance, and pupil responses were monitored at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that this combination of measurements allowed the researchers to test whether extending the exhale did more than simply lower heart rate. They also wanted to determine whether the breathing pattern directly changed how the brain processed potential rewards.

Longer Exhalation Shifted Choices Toward Reward.

According to recent reports, the results demonstrated that extended exhalation slowed heart rate and was associated with riskier choices. Importantly, the change appeared to come from greater attention to possible rewards rather than reduced concern about potential losses. Participants still responded to losses in a similar way.

Sources indicate that the researchers also detected stronger activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. These brain regions are involved in reward processing and in regulating the timing between heartbeats, a measure known as heart rate variability.

"Our study thus underscores the transformative role of breath-based interventions. The interplay between breathing and cardiac dynamics makes the brain more receptive to rewards," explains lead author Wenhao Huang, interpreting the results.

What the Findings Could Mean for Breathing Techniques.

The work adds to a growing field focused on body-brain communication and supports neurovisceral models, which propose that a person's physical state can strongly shape cognitive processes.

According to recent reports, park explains: "Breathing techniques have accompanied humanity for millennia across various religions and cultures. With this study, we provide scientific proof that it is a reliable and targeted method capable of controlling our decisions.".

Because controlled breathing is simple, inexpensive, and relatively easy to learn, the researchers say it could have value as a tool for everyday self-regulation. It may also have potential as a supportive, non-pharmacological approach in clinical settings, particularly for conditions such as anxiety disorders or depression, which can involve disrupted autonomic regulation and altered responses to reward.

Could Breathing Influence Eating Behavior?

Future studies will need to determine whether the same effects appear in broader clinical populations, including people with overweight. The researchers are particularly interested in whether breathing techniques could influence food-related decisions, since eating behavior is strongly affected by both reward processing and a person's physical state.

"Since dietary decisions are strongly influenced by reward assessment and physical state, targeted breath regulation could also play a role in consciously perceiving and more effectively managing eating behavior," Park summarizes for future research activities.

This study was supported by the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space [Grant 01GP2210C (DecEnt-Project), Grant 01EE2301E for the conceptual development of the German Center for Mental Health; Grant 82DZD03D03 (German Center for Diabetes Research)], the Ministry for Science, Research and Culture of the State of Brandenburg (MWFK). Ignacio Rebollo was supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action (MSCA) BRAINSTOM (grant agreement no. 101028203).

Industry News: What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S.
  • “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” noted Jadon Urogdy.
  • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” noted Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Recent findings suggest that urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

According to recent reports, fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

According to recent reports, working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” remarked Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

Sources indicate that natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” mentioned Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related complications than average.

It has been revealed that another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people mentioned the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” remarked Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio remarked. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

#57478. Scientists find a latest layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

Scientists find a latest layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify new avenues for treatment.
  • The study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.
  • To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify new avenues for treatment.

The study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease. Scientists from SCS's Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, and collaborating institutions connected these changes in genome folding with shifts in gene activity and the organization of brain tissue.

To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.

"Alzheimer's disease cannot be understood one layer at a time," noted Jian Ma, the Ray and Stephanie Lane Professor of Computational Biology who led and supervised the study. "The genome's 3D structure is a fundamental regulatory layer that helps to connect DNA sequence to gene activity. By integrating genome folding, cell state, and tissue context, we can move beyond cataloging disease-associated changes toward understanding how they fit together and which mechanisms to test next.".

It has been revealed that DNA does not sit inside a cell as a simple straight strand. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that helps determine which genes are accessible and active. Changes in that physical organization can therefore influence how cells function.

The researchers examined postmortem samples from the prefrontal cortex, an area at the front of the brain. The tissue came from people with and without Alzheimer's disease who had taken part in a long-term dementia study and later donated their brains for research.

Sources indicate that the team used GAGE-seq, a technique that can measure both gene expression and three-dimensional genome contacts within the same individual cell. Those measurements were then combined with spatial transcriptomic maps, which preserve information about where gene activity occurs within intact brain tissue.

By bringing these datasets together, the researchers were able to connect the physical organization of the genome with gene regulation while also seeing where Alzheimer's related molecular and cellular changes appeared within the surrounding tissue.

A New Layer of Alzheimer's Biology.

"Our study represents a major advance in understanding what goes wrong in Alzheimer's disease," said Hansruedi Mathys, assistant professor of neurobiology at Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, who directed the Pitt arm of the study. "We know the classic hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease - accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles - but our results establish higher-order chromatin alterations as a component of the molecular pathology associated with the disease, which currently affects seven million Americans, a number that continues to grow.".

Amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles are among the best known biological features of Alzheimer's disease. The fresh findings suggest that changes in chromatin, the material made of DNA and associated proteins that packages the genome inside cells, should also be considered part of the disease's molecular landscape.

AI Connects Genome Folding to Gene Activity.

Another key part of the research was Hicformer, an artificial intelligence model developed to investigate how genome structure may influence cellular behavior. The model combines DNA sequence information with broad patterns of genome folding and detailed maps showing where different sections of DNA physically contact one another.

Industry observers note that using these inputs, Hicformer predicts gene activity across different types of cells. Xinyue Lu, a doctoral student in Computational Biology who co-led the research, described the system as a computational test bed that can be used to explore how changes in genome folding might alter gene activity.

According to recent reports, "Measuring gene activity and genome folding in the same cell allows us to directly connect chromosome structure with disease-related gene programs," stated Yang Zhang, a project scientist in the Computational Biology Department who co-led the research. "Across several kinds of brain cells, this paired view revealed a consistent signature of 3D genome reorganization in Alzheimer's disease and helped us prioritize regulatory regions for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.".

DNA Organization Becomes Less Distinct.

The researchers identified several consistent differences in the genome architecture of cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.

Industry observers note that large sections of the genome are normally organized into relatively distinct active and inactive regions known as compartments. In Alzheimer's cells, those boundaries appeared less sharply defined. The researchers describe this pattern as "increased compartment mingling.".

Sources indicate that several kinds of brain cells also showed fewer interactions between nearby sections of the genome and more contacts between regions located farther apart. Cells with greater compartment mingling tended to have lower overall levels of gene activity.

According to recent reports, the team also observed weaker interactions between genes and nearby regulatory elements that normally help control whether those genes are switched on or off. At the same time, some contacts across intermediate distances became stronger.

According to recent reports, these structural differences were associated with reduced activity in programs involved in neurons and synapses, along with changes in metabolism and cellular stress responses. The researchers also found links to senescence-related programs in microglia, immune cells in the brain that play crucial roles in maintaining brain health and responding to damage.

Potential Clues for Future Alzheimer's Treatments.

When the researchers mapped these molecular changes across intact brain tissue, they found that the reorganization of the genome was connected not only to altered gene activity but also to differences in how brain cells were arranged within the tissue.

The results establish three-dimensional genome organization as another key layer of Alzheimer's disease biology. They also provide researchers with a framework for testing which changes in genome architecture might directly contribute to the disease.

Future studies can now investigate whether particular structural changes help drive Alzheimer's progression and whether any of the affected regulatory regions could eventually become targets for new therapies.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health. Other CMU authors included doctoral students Shahul Alam and Shike Wang and postdoctoral research associate Junjie Tang. Other Pitt authors include doctoral students Alexander K. Kunisky and Jude Baroudi, post-baccalaureate research fellows Sahar and Sahel Ghorbanikalateh, and visiting scholar Shihan Wang. The team included researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Washington; and the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center.

Latest Update: The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings.
  • But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue.
  • Recent findings suggest that my former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

Recent findings suggest that my former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in massive cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

We have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

First, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

In a recent development, “I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde says. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”.

To get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He says: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Industry observers note that A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

It has been revealed that jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

#57472. Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life.
  • The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India.
  • Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

The Brain's Local Communication Network.

Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

"Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," mentioned Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it.".

Measuring the Brain's Hidden Wiring.

According to recent reports, to investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

The researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

In a recent development, the most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss.

Recent findings suggest that measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

In a recent development, when these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

In a recent development, "The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," mentioned Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition.".

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations.

The researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

In a recent development, the researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

What Scientists Still Need to Learn.

Industry observers note that because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

Long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

"A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," said Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan.".

In addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

Materials provided by Keck School of Medicine of USC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin.
  • It has been revealed that to get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mcDonald's breakfast is a thing of beauty, and if you think we've got it good here in the States, you probably haven't seen what's sitting on Canada's breakfast menu. Alongside familiar faves, you'll find items Americans can't order, the most envy-inducing among them arguably being the Egg BLT McMuffin. Once you hear what's in it, don't be surprised if you catch yourself planning a trip to our northern neighbor.

The Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin. A second version uses nearly identical ingredients but swaps the whole leaves for shredded lettuce. You can only get this variation at McDonald's restaurants located inside Walmart stores — part of a decades-old partnership that once placed roughly 1,000 outposts in the retail chain. McDonald's later closed hundreds of them as drive-thrus became the main source of sales, though Walmart continues to host many locations in Canada.

It has been revealed that to get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative. Your best bet is to start with a Bacon, Egg & Cheese McMuffin, which already ticks off half the ingredients. Ask for a touch of mayo, which gets you close to the sauce of the Canadian original. Since lettuce and tomatoes are lunchtime items, your odds improve near the end of breakfast hours when stores are prepping the lunch menu — you'll likely have to order them at the counter or window.

The Egg BLT might have already convinced you to add McDonald's to your itinerary next time you're in Canada, but it's not the only breakfast item worth the detour. One that caught our eye was the Mighty McGriddles. While the U.S. offers the Bacon, Egg & Cheese and Sausage, Egg & Cheese varieties separately, the Canadian version puts both to shame by stacking a double helping of hickory-smoked bacon, a sausage patty, egg, and cheese between two maple-flavored griddle cakes — a gloriously overstuffed creation that lives up to its name. The Mighty McMuffin follows the same logic, coming loaded with both meats for anyone who can never decide between the two.

Industry observers note that another familiar face on Canadian McDonald's breakfast menus is the bagel, though while America only offers plain, Canada also serves sesame and everything varieties. You can even order one toasted with butter or Philadelphia cream cheese — widely known as the best store-bought brand — as if you're at a proper bagel shop.

Canada's McDonald's restaurants aren't afraid to put a twist on U.S. staples, and they also introduce upcoming items altogether. You won't find chicken anywhere on the standard U.S. breakfast menu, which makes the Chicken McGriddles feel like a curveball up north. The simple yet delicious sandwich pairs a breaded chicken patty with two sweet, maple-flavored griddle cakes for some serious sweet-and-savory fusion.
